title: God as Arjuna's charioteer
hook: Arjuna gives an order to his driver, who is God, and why Hindus love Krishna as Parthasarathi.
carry: god chose to drive arjuna's chariot
tomorrow: from the middle, what does Arjuna actually see?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gita's first chapter rang with conches, and we kept: the shankha sounds as worship begins. When the noise settles, Arjuna speaks.

Before the war, the Mahabharata tells, Arjuna and Duryodhana both came to Krishna for help. Krishna offered a choice: his whole army, or himself alone, promising not to fight. Duryodhana took the army, glad of the deal. Arjuna chose Krishna. And so, on the morning of battle, the one Hindus worship as Vishnu on earth is holding the reins of Arjuna's horses. Then Arjuna speaks to him, and his first words are an instruction to the driver.
screen: `AN ARMY, OR KRISHNA ALONE?` → `ARJUNA CHOSE KRISHNA.` → `AN ORDER TO THE DRIVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the line: senayor ubhayor madhye ratham sthapaya me 'chyuta. Between both armies, set my chariot, Achyuta. Sthapaya: set it, make it stand. An order, spoken to God. And Krishna simply does it. Sanjaya says Hrishikesha drove the chariot into the middle and stopped it before Bhishma and Drona. Hindus have loved this moment for centuries, and they have a name for Krishna in it: Parthasarathi, the charioteer of Partha, Arjuna. In Chennai, an old and famous temple, Parthasarathy, honors him in just that role. Why love it? Because it shows what bhakti, loving devotion, believes about God: the highest Lord can choose to come close, as a friend, even as a servant, to someone who chose him. Duryodhana wanted Krishna's power. Arjuna wanted Krishna. Many teachers also hear an older image behind the scene. The Katha Upanishad pictures the self as the rider, the body as the chariot, the intellect as the driver, the mind as the reins and the senses as the horses. In the Gita, the one at the reins is God. Readers take Arjuna's madhye, in the middle, two ways: a warrior wanting a clear view, or a man placing himself exactly between two sides that are both his family. Either way, he doesn't go there alone. That's the teaching for a hard day now: in Hindu faith, God isn't only far above. God can be sitting at the front of the chariot, steering where you've asked to go.
screen: `SET MY CHARIOT. KRISHNA OBEYS.` · `PARTHASARATHI: ARJUNA'S DRIVER.` · `BHAKTI: GOD COMES CLOSE.` · `THE CHARIOT IMAGE, GOD AT THE REINS.` · then, large: `GOD TAKES THE REINS.`

segments.voice: Sit in the very middle of your seat, weight even, left and right. If you pray, picture Krishna at the front of the chariot, reins in hand, and quietly hand him one thing you're carrying today; some people say a name as they do it, Govinda, or Parthasarathi. If you don't pray, picture a steady driver you trust, and let your hands rest open in your lap. When a thought pulls you to one side, come back to the middle, and breathe.
Madhye: in the middle, where Arjuna asks to be set. And Parthasarathi: Krishna as Arjuna's charioteer, God holding the reins.
Your line: god chose to drive arjuna's chariot. Arjuna chose him over an army. Until tomorrow.
